headlines.html: China Mobile enters orbital edge computing: On August 18, China Mobile's "Space Intelligent Computing Payload 1.0" flew alongside the Honghu-03 satellite on Landspace's Zhuque-3 recovery flight, marking the Chinese telecom giant's first demonstration of distributed computing in orbit. On the same flight, the Zhuque-3 first stage became the world's third — after SpaceX and Blue Origin — to achieve a ground legged landing — (SpaceNews)

White House unveils first new space transportation policy in 13 years: Setting a goal of supporting 1,000 launches and reentries per year from U.S. facilities by 2030, the policy focuses on expanding launch and reentry infrastructure rather than launch vehicles themselves — (SpaceNews)

2026-08-22.summary_html:
① China Mobile (SpaceNews, 8/21) — Landspace's second Zhuque-3 flight on August 18 carried China Mobile's "Space Intelligent Computing Payload 1.0" into orbit alongside the Honghu-03 satellite. Jointly developed by the Institute of Computing Technology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and Hongqing Technology, Landspace's satellite-manufacturing subsidiary, the payload runs a domestically built lightweight satellite-borne core network and onboard "agent" software. It is the first payload China Mobile has put into orbit targeting distributed edge computing, bringing the Chinese telecom giant into the orbital computing race alongside ADA Space's Three-Body Constellation and Tianguang. On the same flight, the Zhuque-3 first stage touched down on its legs at the Minqin landing site in Gansu province, marking the first ground recovery by a Chinese company and the world's third legged landing of an orbital-class booster. Landspace aims to conduct a reflight test of the recovered first stage within six months, with the stage designed for at least 20 reuses.

② White House (SpaceNews, 8/20) — On August 20, the White House released its national space transportation policy, revised for the first time since 2013. It sets a goal of supporting 1,000 launches and reentries per year from U.S. facilities by 2030 — a fivefold increase over the fewer than 200 U.S.-based launches in 2025. The emphasis is on infrastructure rather than launch vehicles: it directs the Department of Defense and NASA to improve launch sites and pursue joint development with the private sector, and it orders a search for additional launch site candidates, the establishment of federal launch site scheduling criteria within 180 days, and the designation of priority airspace for launch corridors. Targeting the reentry bottleneck as well, it calls for identifying new federal reentry sites within 90 days. The measure builds on last year's commercial space executive order and a July 30 FAA proposed rule that would exempt launch and launch site licensing from 13 environmental laws. The same day saw the United States and China pushing the foundations of orbital computing up from opposite ends. China is building from the bottom up — with a reusable launch vehicle and an actual on-orbit computing demonstration by a telecom giant — while the United States widens the deployment pipeline through top-down policy aimed at launch and reentry bottlenecks. China Mobile joining an orbital computing field previously dominated by startups (ADA Space, Tianguang) as a state-scale carrier signals that this competition is moving from the experimental stage to the industrial stage. The U.S. goal of 1,000 launches per year targets the launch capacity that future orbital data center constellations — Starcloud, Project Sunrise, SpaceX AI satellites — will ultimately have to rely on. To be honest, though, neither a reusable rocket nor a launch policy is itself an orbital data center — one is the launch economy that will carry orbital computing, the other is the real ODC core payload riding on top of it, and today's center of gravity lies with China Mobile.

headlines.html: Muon Space closes $250 million Series C: Smallsat manufacturer Muon Space enters unicorn status at a $1.5 billion valuation, investing in 500-satellites-per-year output at its new San Jose plant and in expanding a large satellite platform for orbital data centers — (SpaceNews)

2026-08-21.summary_html: ① Muon Space (SpaceNews, 8/20) — Muon Space, a Mountain View, California satellite manufacturer, closed a $250 million Series C round on August 20. The round was led by Eclipse Capital, which co-led True Anomaly's $650 million round earlier this year, and according to people familiar with the matter the company was valued at $1.5 billion, joining this year's run of "space unicorns." Now in its fifth year, the company has launched 11 satellites to date and will scale its recently opened San Jose factory to 500 satellites per year by 2027 — a tenfold increase over its previous capacity. Total funding raised has now surpassed $386 million, and the company emphasized its vertically integrated "Mission Foundry" model, which handles 95% of production in-house. The key thread is the orbital data center connection: Muon said its Starship-class large platform "Condor Ultra," unveiled in June, is designed with 20 kilowatts of baseline power and more than 18 square meters of nadir-facing payload area to meet "emerging demand for orbital data centers," with a debut targeted for 2028. Muon's latest round sits on the same axis as the recent trend of Apex Space (valued at $2.3 billion) and K2 Space ($6.8 billion) raising a combined $700 million. All three companies started from small buses and are moving up to larger satellites that carry more power and compute, and this competition to scale up and mass-produce is precisely the supply base that must be in place for orbital data centers to actually operate. Satellite manufacturers are not data centers themselves, but constellation concepts — SpaceX aiming for 100 times the scale of Starlink, Project Sunrise's 51,600 satellites, and Orbital's 100,000 — will ultimately be decided by "who can churn out large compute satellites at scale." CEO Jonny Dyer's remark that "as industries increasingly rely on space-based intelligence, communications and compute, it accelerates next-generation space infrastructure" shows that this capital is aimed beyond small satellites for observation and communications, at the hardware layer of the orbital compute era.

headlines.html: Landspace successfully recovers Zhuque-3 booster: China's private Landspace completed its second orbital launch of the reusable methane rocket Zhuque-3, landing the first stage on its legs. It becomes the world's third entity to recover an orbital-class booster on legs, after SpaceX and Blue Origin — (SpaceNews)

U.S. Space Force signs orbital data-network demo deal with Rocket Lab: A 2027 in-orbit test of multi-vendor interoperability for a space data network, linking the SpaceX backbone and third-party satellites via optical links — (SpaceNews)

2026-08-20.summary_html:
① Landspace (SpaceNews, 8/18) — Chinese private launch provider Landspace vertically landed the first-stage booster of its Zhuque-3 rocket at a landing site in Gansu province, 390 kilometers downrange, during the vehicle's second orbital launch on August 18. It is the world's third entity, after SpaceX and Blue Origin, to recover an orbital-class booster on legs. The stainless-steel rocket measures 4.5 meters in diameter with a liftoff mass in the 570-ton class and is powered by nine Tianque methane engines; with first-stage recovery it lifts 18.3 tons to low Earth orbit — a payload capacity comparable to the Falcon 9. The Honghu-3 satellite carried on this flight was built by Hongqing, Landspace's satellite-manufacturing subsidiary, which raised $191 million last month.

② Rocket Lab (SpaceNews, 8/18) — Rocket Lab announced on August 18 that it will demonstrate the U.S. Space Force's space data network in orbit in 2027. Under the $12 million contract, it will fly optical-communications and networking equipment on a Photon satellite to test interoperability between the backbone SpaceX is building for $2.29 billion and third-party satellites. The Space Force allocated $12 million each to five companies — Rocket Lab, Amazon, Lockheed Martin, Northrop and York — for a total of $60 million, aiming to create a common interface that avoids dependence on any single vendor. The data network is a military communications system that routes high-volume data between satellites over optical links. The two stories mark progress on the two preconditions underpinning orbital data centers — the ability to launch satellites cheaply and in bulk, and the ability to move high-volume data around in orbit. Landspace's reusability success is launch infrastructure that drives down the cost of deploying megaconstellations (Zhuque-3 and the Honghu satellites are not data centers themselves, but the industrial foundation that makes them possible), while the Space Force's data network is the interconnect layer that binds scattered satellites into one. One side is China's commercial launch competition, the other America's military standardization — two contrasting U.S. and Chinese approaches to preparing for the era of orbital compute, revealed side by side.

headlines.html: Blue Origin's second launch pad: Groundbreaking begins at Cape Canaveral on LC-36B, a pad dedicated to the new New Glenn 9x4 variant — a deployment foothold for the 51,600-satellite Project Sunrise orbital compute constellation (SpaceNews)
CesiumAstro acquires a chipmaker: Buys RF beamforming chip designer Zariot Technologies, bringing silicon in-house for its 737-satellite constellation (SpaceNews)

The spacecraft-design bottleneck shifts: With launch costs falling, surface area, power, and heat rejection — not mass — become the new constraints, the very physics limits that orbital data centers face (SpaceNews)

2026-08-15.summary_html:
① Blue Origin (SpaceNews, 8/14) — Blue Origin announced it will build a second launch pad, LC-36B, at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station. Dedicated to the new New Glenn 9x4 variant, it stacks nine BE-4 engines beneath four BE-3U engines, a configuration that dramatically increases thrust over the current LC-36A's 7x2 layout. A vertical integration building and a payload processing facility will rise alongside it; the U.S. Space Force awarded a $78.2 million contract for the payload processing facility last October. The article makes no mention of data centers, but New Glenn is the only heavy-lift vehicle capable of carrying Blue Origin's own 51,600-satellite Project Sunrise — an orbital compute constellation. The decision to double the pads and scale up the variant directly governs how fast that constellation can be deployed.

② CesiumAstro (SpaceNews, 8/13) — Satellite communications firm CesiumAstro acquired chip designer Zariot Technologies. Founded in 2015, Zariot works on RF chips and digital beamforming technology for satellite communications, electronic warfare, and radar, and roughly 100 employees in the United States and Switzerland join CesiumAstro. The acquisition price was not disclosed. That silicon capability will feed CesiumAstro's planned 737-satellite Synchronicity low-Earth-orbit constellation and its Element satellite platform, whose first launch is set for October. Following its acquisition of AI startup Vidrover late last year, the move is part of a vertical-integration push, reflecting a broader trend of the satellite industry taking control of the chip design that determines communications and compute performance.

③ SpaceNews analysis (SpaceNews, 8/14) — The analysis argues that as launch costs fall, the spacecraft-design bottleneck has shifted from mass to surface area. Power now governs sensing, computation, communications, and thermal control alike, and every additional watt requires that much more collecting area and radiating area. Fairing volume, however, stays the same, increasing the burden and failure risk of the deployment mechanisms that fold in solar panels and radiators. Boeing's Q4S chose a particular platform because of sustained power, and SES's O3b mPOWER identified power as the limiting factor in the medium-Earth-orbit radiation environment. It is precisely the same power and heat-rejection constraint that orbital data centers face. Today's three stories are not new announcements about any specific orbital data center, but rather illuminate all at once the three pillars of the industrial base — launch capacity, silicon, and physical design — that would actually build such a data center. Blue Origin buys orbital-insertion speed for its own megaconstellation by adding a launch pad, while CesiumAstro brings chip design in-house, joining the "who holds the satellite silicon" race that runs through Intel Starfire (8/11) and SpaceX-Nvidia (8/7). And the analysis that surface area, power, and heat rejection are the new bottleneck is a reminder that the fundamental constraint on orbital compute is, in the end, thermodynamics. Communications constellations and launch infrastructure are not data centers in themselves, but no orbital data center holds together without the premise of mass-producing and deploying low-cost satellites at scale. While core new announcements have been quiet this week, the competition is proceeding quietly at this supply-chain layer.

headlines.html: China's iSpace lands $148 million first tranche of Series E for reusable rocketry: Interstellar Glory (iSpace) has secured roughly 1 billion yuan for mass production of its Hyperbola-3 reusable launch vehicle and sea-recovery infrastructure — (SpaceNews)

Firefly pushes launch dates back even as rocket production hits an all-time high: Alpha production has climbed to record levels alongside development of the larger Eclipse, with "launch capacity never in shorter supply" — (SpaceNews)

2026-08-14.summary_html:
① iSpace (SpaceNews, 8/12) — Chinese commercial launch firm Interstellar Glory has raised roughly $148 million, or 1 billion yuan, as the first tranche of its Series E round. The funds will go toward research and mass production of the Hyperbola-3 reusable launch vehicle, production capacity for its Focus-2 methane–liquid oxygen engine, launch and sea-recovery infrastructure, and preliminary research on a heavy-lift launch vehicle. The round was led by an asset manager affiliated with a major Chinese state-owned bank, directly reflecting the central government's push to elevate commercial space to a strategic industry. Coming on the heels of a record $729 million raise this past February, Hyperbola-3 is reported to carry a low-Earth-orbit payload capacity in the 8,500-kilogram class.

② Firefly Aerospace (SpaceNews, 8/11) — In its August 11 earnings report, Firefly said production of its small launch vehicle Alpha is at "an all-time high." CEO Jason Kim said demand for launch capacity is "exploding right now, and launch capability has never been this constrained," adding that both Alpha and the larger Eclipse in development are seeing strong demand. Actual launches, however, have not kept pace with production: Alpha has flown just seven times since 2021, and Flight 8 — the first flight of the stretched Block 2 upgrade — has slipped to the fourth quarter. Today was less about orbital data centers themselves than about the U.S. and China moving in parallel on the launch and manufacturing base that will carry them. An orbital data center is ultimately a constellation of thousands to tens of thousands of satellites, so the ability to launch satellites cheaply and in bulk is its precondition — reusable rockets and mass satellite production are not the ODC itself but the supply chain that makes it possible. China is pouring state-bank capital into reusable launch vehicles and sea recovery, laying the groundwork for domestic mega-constellations like Guowang, Qianfan and Honghu-3, and beyond that for orbital-compute ambitions such as Three-Body Computing and Star-Compute. America's Firefly, meanwhile, has ramped production to record highs on overflowing commercial demand, yet exposes the opposite bottleneck, with its launch cadence unable to keep up. Each side, in its own way, showed that whoever first bends the cost and cycle time of launch is where the real contest of the orbital-compute era will be decided.

headlines.html: China's "Three-Body Computing Constellation" demonstrates 192 hours of continuous satellite-to-satellite laser link: ADA Space and Zhejiang Lab maintained an uninterrupted laser communication link between two orbiting satellites for more than eight days, running computing tasks simultaneously while the link stayed up. It is a real-world demonstration of the "always-on connectivity" that lets multiple satellites collaborate as one in an orbital cloud — (China in Space)

China launches space AI data center project with "Tianguang-1" experimental satellite: Launched in late July, Tianguang-1 is demonstrating thermal dissipation and power management in orbit, with the goal of building a 12-satellite space AI data center by 2027. The state-led plan has entered its first hardware phase — (hellodd)

Sophia Space and Caltech secure U.S. patent for space-based data center: They obtained U.S. Patent No. 12,679,564 for a modular space data center architecture that is solar-powered and cooled by deep-space radiative cooling. It marks progress in cementing orbital compute as defensible intellectual property — (TipRanks)

2026-08-13.summary_html:
① China in Space (7/29) — China's ADA Space and Zhejiang Lab announced they had successfully maintained a laser communication link between two orbiting satellites for 192 hours, 8 minutes and 45 seconds — more than eight days — without interruption. Transmission availability reached 99.99%, the maximum distance between the two satellites was 1,000 kilometers, and the two-way transmission rate peaked at 100 gigabits per second. The key point is that throughout the time the link was maintained, the satellites ran computing tasks together across dozens of orbital revolutions. This demonstrated the precondition for an "orbital cloud" — always-on connectivity — that distributes computations too heavy for a single satellite across multiple units. The laser terminals were supplied by HiStarlink, and this Three-Body Computing Constellation, which had its first launch in May 2025, currently has 12 satellites in orbit and is preparing a second batch targeting 2,800 satellites by 2035. Tencent, Alibaba Cloud, and SenseTime are among the participants.

② hellodd (8/9) — China has actually begun its space AI data center project with the late-July launch of the Tianguang-1 experimental satellite. Tianguang-1 is a standard module with computing power on par with a single ground server, tasked with validating the thermal dissipation and power management a data center needs in orbit. The Beijing Aerospace Future Space Technology Research Institute, which leads the plan, has set the goal of placing 12 AI data center satellites in orbit by 2027 to achieve 200 petaflops per second of performance, and a total of 64 megawatts by 2030. Behind this lies a data bottleneck: currently less than 5% of the data generated by observation satellites with 10-centimeter resolution can be sent down to the ground, so the aim is to process imaging and analysis directly in orbit. If the earlier Three-Body Constellation proved satellite-to-satellite connectivity, Tianguang-1 shows that national resources have been committed to the physical bottleneck of managing heat and power within a single satellite.

③ TipRanks (7/14) — Sophia Space, jointly with Caltech, obtained U.S. Patent No. 12,679,564 for the modular architecture of a space-based data center. The patent was filed in October 2024 and registered on July 14, 2026, and is jointly owned by Sophia and Caltech. At its core is a large-scale, solar-powered modular architecture that passively radiates waste heat into deep space instead of using ground-style mechanical cooling. Rather than beaming power down to the ground, it keeps computation in orbit and sends only the resulting data back to Earth — inverting the technical direction of Caltech's Space Solar Power project, which transmitted wireless power from space to Earth. This patent is a core asset in Sophia's tile-based modular compute platform strategy, and it originated in the high-risk, high-reward research of the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, which Caltech operates. (The same patent was already covered in a July 30 SpaceNews announcement; today's is follow-up reporting after the patent number was confirmed.) Today's three stories show where the two physical bottlenecks of orbital data centers — the connectivity linking satellites to one another, and the heat and power within each satellite — are being solved right now. China is pushing both bottlenecks with national resources at once, physically proving the always-on laser link needed for multiple satellites to compute as one via the Three-Body Constellation, and the thermal dissipation and power management inside a single satellite via Tianguang-1. The United States, by contrast, leans toward staking out solutions to the same problems through defensible intellectual property and startup designs, as with the Sophia-Caltech patent. The contrast between state-led hardware demonstration and venture-led design and patent land-grabbing reveals that the orbital compute race is moving past concepts into an actual deployment phase.

headlines.html: Europe warned of orbital compute gap: The European Space Policy Institute (ESPI) released a report warning that "Europe risks falling behind the United States and China in orbital data centers and becoming dependent on foreign infrastructure," recommending an EU-level flagship ODC program under its 2028–2034 research framework. — (SpaceNews)

California emerges as satellite mass-production hub: Despite cost and regulatory pressures, California has drawn one-third of U.S. space-tech companies and more than half of all space venture investment over the past five years to become a satellite mass-manufacturing hub, according to an analysis. Muon Space is running a 12,000-square-meter factory targeting 500 satellites a year. — (SpaceNews)

2026-08-06.summary_html:
① ESPI (SpaceNews, 8/5) — A report published by the European Space Policy Institute on August 5 warned that Europe could fall behind the United States and China in the orbital data center race and become dependent on foreign orbital compute infrastructure. The report identifies China as the frontrunner. In a coordinated push linking national policy, local governments, and state-owned enterprises, ADAspace's Three-Body Computing Constellation plans 2,800 satellites after launching 12 last May, while Shanghai's Xingshu Tiansuan network began deploying a 1,000-satellite fleet this July. In the United States, Starcloud and Cowboy Space are each attracting private capital at valuations exceeding $1 billion. Europe, by contrast, remains stuck in research and small-scale demonstrations — apart from the French startup Alatir, which is pursuing a robotically assembled ODC — with no large-scale deployment strategy, the report noted. ESPI recommended launching an EU flagship ODC program under the 2028–2034 research framework, having the EU and ESA serve as early customers, holding a "European ODC Challenge," and forming an international standards working group.

② California satellite manufacturing (SpaceNews, 8/5) — An industry analysis published the same day shows where the satellite mass-production base underpinning orbital data centers is concentrated. California is home to one-third of U.S. space-tech companies, more than half of all U.S. space venture investment over the past five years, and 10,000 aerospace engineers. Muon Space is targeting production of 500 satellites a year at a 12,000-square-meter factory, and the state is holding manufacturers in place with tax credits — $32.75 million for Vast, $24 million for Apex, and $12.7 million for True Anomaly. Among them is K2 Space, which is pursuing gigawatt-class satellite buses for orbital data centers. A mass-production base for communications and observation satellites is not itself an ODC, but since no orbital compute constellation is viable without cheap, high-volume satellites, this manufacturing density is the substance of the supply-chain advantage the United States holds. The two articles that appeared side by side on August 5 show two sides of the same axis — that the orbital data center race has now moved beyond the technology-demonstration stage into industrial and policy competition between nations. The ESPI report points to the policy vacuum: China is pushing hard as a state to seize standards, and U.S. venture capital is minting unicorns, while only Europe remains trapped in research with no coordinated deployment strategy. The California article shows, in concrete terms, where that U.S. advantage comes from — the manufacturing density that concentrates talent and capital in one place to churn out hundreds of satellites a year is the precondition for an ODC constellation. What Europe envies is exactly what California has: the policy gap and the industrial agglomeration are two faces of the same coin.

headlines.html: Spain commits up to €2 billion to IRIS² sovereign military satellite network: Spain has allocated up to €2 billion (about $2.3 billion) to build a national military satellite communications network tied into Europe's own IRIS² constellation, making it the largest single-nation backer — (SpaceNews)

U.S. Space Force awards K2 Space $22.9 million for satellite-to-satellite laser communications demo: K2 Space, which builds gigawatt-class buses for orbital data centers, has won a contract to demonstrate optical communications terminals that let satellites exchange data directly with one another — (SpaceNews)

2026-08-03.summary_html:
① Spanish Ministry of Defense (SpaceNews, 7/31) — Spain will invest between €1.6 billion and €2 billion in a national military satellite communications network to be integrated into IRIS², the European Union's low- and medium-Earth-orbit communications constellation. The figure surpasses the roughly $750 million pledged days earlier by Poland, making Spain the largest single-nation backer of IRIS². With a total program cost of €10.6 billion and a fleet of about 292 satellites, IRIS² is targeting full operation by 2030, and Spain will directly secure six medium-orbit and six low-orbit satellites along with a ground gateway station. The Ministry of Defense said the budget covers "the space segment, ground control, and the entire lifecycle of system operations." It is not an orbital data center in itself, but it reflects Europe's move to build sovereign infrastructure for mass-producing and operating satellites.

② K2 Space (SpaceNews, 8/1) — The U.S. Space Force is paying K2 Space $22.9 million to demonstrate satellite-to-satellite laser communications. K2 will procure, integrate, launch, and operate two of its own satellites fitted with the "Enterprise Space Terminal," with completion targeted for 2028. These optical terminals beam data directly between satellites without routing through a ground station, and they form part of the "space data network" the Department of Defense is pursuing to rapidly share missile-warning, tracking, and targeting information across a multi-orbit distributed surveillance layer. K2, which raised a $500 million Series D last week on the strength of its gigawatt-class large buses for orbital data centers, is with this optical demonstration validating the satellite-to-satellite optical backbone technology that any orbital compute constellation will require. Today's two stories are not about the "nodes" of an orbital data center but about the infrastructure and capital underpinning them. Spain's €2 billion speaks to who builds and owns the constellation — Europe's sovereignty over satellite mass production and operation — while K2's optical communications contract validates the optical backbone that carries data between satellites without a ground station. Neither is a data center in itself; both serve communications and defense. But mass-produced satellites and satellite-to-satellite optical networks are the precondition on which every orbital compute vision stands, whether SpaceX's million-satellite orbital data center or Starcloud's 88,000. While core headlines like Sophia Space's patents and regulatory debates take the front row, government and defense money is quietly flowing into the industrial base and optical backbone beneath them.

headlines.html: Orbital data center constellations need "rules of the road": As orbital data center plans on the scale of Starcloud's 88,000 satellites and SpaceX's 1 million take shape, a Washington policy panel warned that space traffic coordination standards to prevent satellite collisions must be established now — (SpaceNews)

2026-08-01.summary_html: ① SpaceNews (SpaceNews, 7/30) — At a July 29 panel hosted by the Secure World Foundation in Washington, Starcloud co-founder and chief technology officer Ezra Feilden, along with officials from The Aerospace Corporation, Planet, and the U.S. Commerce Department's Office of Space Commerce, raised the question of traffic management for orbital data center constellations. Starcloud has filed for 88,000 satellites and SpaceX for as many as 1 million, and the analysis warns that satellite avoidance maneuvers — currently running in the hundreds of thousands per year — could surge to roughly 500 million per year in a 1-million-satellite era. The dawn-dusk sun-synchronous orbits where data center satellites are expected to cluster are of particular concern, since every satellite must travel in the same direction; Feilden warned it would be "like a highway where no one has decided which lane to drive in — the risk of head-on collisions would be enormous." Participants proposed that industry set its own standards ahead of government-mandated regulation, through the Commerce Department's build-out of TraCSS, a space traffic coordination system modeled on air traffic control, and through the Space Commerce certification program, which is currently voluntary.
